questions.question: Which broad area takes the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, including pensions and benefits

questions.why: HM Treasury PESA consistently shows social protection as the largest function of public spending.

questions.question: Over recent decades, how has UK public spending on health compared with spending on defence?

options.A: Health spending has been much larger
options.B: Defence spending has been much larger
options.D: Health is not paid from public money

questions.why: HM Treasury PESA shows health spending has been several times larger than defence spending throughout recent decades.

questions.question: In recent years, total UK public spending has been roughly what share of the size of the economy (GDP)?
questions.why: OBR and ONS figures put total managed expenditure at around 40 to 45% of GDP.

questions.question: Health spending rose 50% in cash over a decade. What else do you need to know to say whether it grew in real terms?

options.A: How much prices rose over the same period
options.D: Nothing; cash growth is real growth

questions.why: Real-terms change removes inflation, so cash growth alone cannot show real growth.

questions.question: Which tax raises the most money for the UK government?
questions.why: HMRC receipts show income tax is the largest single tax.

questions.question: Which of these is government income but not a tax?

options.C: Interest and dividends the government receives

questions.why: ONS public sector finances count interest and dividends as non-tax receipts, separate from taxes and from borrowing.

questions.question: When the government spends more than it receives in a year, how is the gap mainly covered?

options.C: By cutting the State Pension that year
options.D: The gap is simply left unpaid

questions.why: The shortfall is public sector net borrowing, which is borrowing rather than a tax or receipt.

questions.question: Which of these is collected by local councils rather than HMRC?
questions.why: Council tax is set and collected by local authorities.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax is paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers?
questions.why: HMRC statistics show the top 1% have paid roughly a quarter to under a third of income tax for many years.

questions.question: If the top 1% pay about 28% of all income tax, what does that tell you?

options.A: Their personal income tax rate is 28%
options.B: Their share of total income tax receipts is about 28%
options.C: They pay 28% of all taxes of every kind
options.D: 28% of people are in the top 1%

questions.why: A share of revenue is not the same as a personal tax rate or a share of all taxes.

questions.question: According to ONS, which income group pays the highest share of its disposable income in indirect taxes like VAT?

options.D: All groups pay exactly the same share

questions.why: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits shows indirect taxes take a larger share of disposable income for poorer households.

questions.question: According to ONS, how do direct taxes as a share of gross income change as household income rises?
questions.why: ONS data show direct taxes such as income tax take a rising share of gross income in higher-income groups.

questions.question: Which of these is an indirect tax?
questions.why: VAT is charged on spending, making it an indirect tax; ONS treats the others as direct taxes.

questions.question: ONS says an average household pays a certain percentage of gross income in all taxes. What is this figure?

options.B: The share of all UK tax revenue households pay
options.C: An average across households of direct and indirect taxes relative to household income
options.D: The top rate of income tax

questions.why: A household average combines several taxes and people, so it is neither a personal rate nor a share of revenue.

questions.question: A page shows an example family paying £8,000 tax a year, labelled as an illustration. How should you treat that number?

options.B: As a worked example based on stated assumptions, not a measurement
options.C: As the tax every family pays

questions.why: Illustrations are calculations from assumptions and must be kept separate from measured statistics.

questions.question: Which official source measures taxes and benefits across UK household income groups?

options.B: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits on household income
options.D: Bank of England interest rate decisions

questions.why: This ONS release estimates direct and indirect taxes and benefits by household income group.

questions.question: Average pay rose 5% in a year while prices rose 7%. What happened to real pay?
questions.why: Real pay growth is roughly cash pay growth minus inflation.

questions.question: Since the late 1970s, how has manufacturing's share of UK jobs changed?

options.C: It has stayed about the same

questions.why: ONS workforce jobs show manufacturing fell from roughly a quarter of jobs around 1978 to under one in ten today.

questions.question: Employment rose after a new policy started. What can a chart of employment alone tell you?
questions.why: A change over time does not by itself show its cause.

questions.question: What is the most common housing tenure for households in England?
questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows about two thirds of households own their home.

questions.question: Since the early 2000s, how has the share of English households renting privately changed?

options.A: It has fallen to almost zero
options.C: It has stayed exactly the same

questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows private renting roughly doubled from around one in ten households.

questions.question: Which country do UK residents visit most often on trips abroad?
questions.why: ONS Travel trends consistently show Spain as the most visited country by UK residents.

questions.question: In England, what is the legal maximum for infant classes (ages 5 to 7) with one teacher?
questions.why: English infant class size law limits classes taught by one qualified teacher to 30 pupils.

questions.question: A survey has no data for 2020 and changed definitions in 2021. How should a chart show this?

options.C: Show the gap and mark the definition change

questions.why: Missing years and breaks must be shown explicitly, never filled with zero or interpolated.
